title: Planted by the Water
subtitle: Psalms 1–41 in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
The Psalms are the Bible's own prayer book: songs for sleepless nights and bright mornings, for running from enemies and running toward God. The first forty-one of them make up Book One of the Psalter, most of them written by David, shepherd and king.

This volume answers them one at a time, forty short poems in five parts, each beside a picture and under a single line from the psalm it answers. The honest ones stay honest. How long? is a prayer too.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Keep the Psalms open alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Like a Tree
parts.epigraph: He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water
parts.lightHint: Near 'planted' (Psalm 1:1–3) in Part 1: Like a Tree

parts.title: How Long?
parts.epigraph: How long, Yahweh? Will you forget me forever?
parts.lightHint: Near 'a high tower' (Psalm 9:9–10) in Part 2: How Long?

parts.title: The Shepherd
parts.epigraph: Y ahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing.
parts.lightHint: Near 'my lamp' (Psalm 18:1–28) in Part 3: The Shepherd

parts.title: Wait for the Lord
parts.epigraph: W ait for Y ahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage.
parts.lightName: Light of Wait for the Lord
parts.lightHint: Near 'I love your house' (Psalm 26:8) in Part 4: Wait for the Lord

parts.lightHint: Near 'near' (Psalm 34:8–18) in Part 5: Taste and See

paintings.title: planted
paintings.epigraph: “that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither”
paintings.poem:
the Psalms open
not with a song
but with a tree.

roots in the stream.
fruit when it's time.
leaves that stay green
in the dry months.

no hurry.
no striving.
just planted
where the water is.

that's the whole book
in a picture:
stay near the water.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“the Psalms open not with a song but with a tree”) and the closing thought (“that's the whole book in a picture: stay near the water”), what is Psalm 1:1–3 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: heaven laughs
paintings.epigraph: “Blessed are all those who take refuge in him.”
paintings.poem:
the nations rage.
kings plot.
the headlines shout.

and heaven
laughs.

not a cruel laugh—
the calm of someone
who already knows
how it ends.

the psalm's last word
is a door left open:
blessed are all
who take refuge in him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Planted by the Water, “heaven laughs” (Psalm 2:1–12) slows us down at the open threshold to remind us: “the psalm's last word is a door left open: blessed are all who take refuge in him.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: I slept
paintings.epigraph: “I laid myself down and slept. I awakened; for Yahweh sustains me.”
paintings.poem:
David wrote this
running from his own son.

enemies everywhere.
voices saying
God won't help him.

and then this line:
I lay down.
I slept.
I woke up.

sometimes the bravest prayer
is closing your eyes
and trusting someone else
to keep watch.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “I slept” (Psalm 3:1–5), what would you talk about after reading, “sometimes the bravest prayer is closing your eyes and trusting someone else to keep watch”?

paintings.title: lie down anyway
paintings.epigraph: “In peace I will both lay myself down and sleep”
paintings.poem:
night again.

the worries line up
at the foot of the bed
like creditors.

and the psalm says:
lie down anyway.
in peace.

not because the list is gone.
because you,
Lord, alone,
keep me safe.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet centerpiece of “lie down anyway”: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “lie down anyway”—“because you, Lord, alone, keep me safe”?

paintings.title: watch
paintings.epigraph: “In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.”
paintings.poem:
in the morning
I lay it out—

like a farmer laying out seed,
like a priest laying wood on the altar—

and then I watch.

prayer isn't
throwing words into the air
and walking off.

it's setting them down
and looking up
to see what he'll do.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the unhewn stones of the altar in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “it's setting them down and looking up to see what he'll do” (Psalm 5:1–3)?

paintings.title: every night
paintings.epigraph: “Every night I flood my bed. I drench my couch with my tears.”
paintings.poem:
this is in the Bible:
a grown man
crying every night
until the pillow is soaked.

no one tells him
to cheer up.

God keeps the prayer
in the book,

and a few lines later,
David says:
the Lord has heard my weeping.

your tears
are not too much
for him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Psalm 6:6–9, the story turns on the tears God keeps in His bottle—and ends with, “your tears are not too much for him.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: my shield
paintings.epigraph: “My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart.”
paintings.poem:
he'd been accused,
slandered,
chased.

and he didn't hide
behind his reputation,
or his own defense.

my shield
is with God.

let him
take the hits.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Psalm 7:10 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “my shield” and whispers, “and he didn't hide behind his reputation, or his own defense. let him take the hits.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: the work of your fingers
paintings.epigraph: “When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars”
paintings.poem:
a shepherd boy
on a hillside at night,
looking up.

the moon.
the stars.
the work of God's fingers—
not even his arms,
his fingers.

and the question
that still undoes us:

who are we,
that you remember us?

and yet
he does.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “and the question that still undoes us: who are we, that you remember us? and yet he does.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: a high tower
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh will also be a high tower for the oppressed”
paintings.poem:
for the oppressed—
not the powerful,
not the ones who already have walls—

a high tower.

God builds his strongest places
where the weakest people
need them.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “God builds his strongest places where the weakest people need them” (Psalm 9:9–10) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: far off
paintings.epigraph: “Why do you stand far off, Yahweh?”
paintings.poem:
why are you so far away?
why do you hide
when it's hardest?

the Bible lets us ask that.
out loud.
in worship.

and the same psalm, a little later:
but you do see.
you take it in hand.
you help the fatherless.

both lines are prayer.
the question
and the trust.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “far off” (Psalm 10:1–14): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “the question and the trust”?

paintings.title: flee like a bird
paintings.epigraph: “How can you say to my soul, “Flee as a bird to your mountain”?”
paintings.poem:
run! they said.
fly to the mountains
like a bird.
the foundations are cracking.

and David said:
I've already taken refuge.

not in the mountains.
in the Lord.

you don't have to run
to be safe.
you have to know
where you're standing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Psalm 11:1–3 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “you have to know where you're standing” in your own story?

paintings.title: seven times
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh’s words are flawless words, as silver refined in a clay furnace, purified seven times.”
paintings.poem:
everyone lies,
the psalm begins.
flattery. double talk.
smooth lips.

and against all that noise:
God's words—

silver,
refined seven times,
nothing false left in them.

when everything is spin,
there is one voice
you can take
at its word.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “seven times” (Psalm 12:1–6), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the still, unhurried voice after reading, “when everything is spin, there is one voice you can take at its word”?

paintings.title: how long?
paintings.epigraph: “How long will you hide your face from me?”
paintings.poem:
how long?
four times in two verses.

how long will you forget me?
how long will you hide?
how long this ache?
how long?

and then, with nothing changed,
the turn:

but I trust
in your loving kindness.

sometimes faith
doesn't wait for the answer.
it sings
before it comes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“how long? four times in two verses”) and the closing thought (“and then, with nothing changed, the turn: but I trust in your loving kindness. it sings before it comes”), what is Psalm 13:1–6 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: good neighbor
paintings.epigraph: “who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?”
paintings.poem:
who gets to live
near God?

the answer isn't
the most religious.

it's the one who
tells the truth,
keeps his word even when it costs him,
doesn't slander his neighbor,
doesn't take a bribe.

holiness,
it turns out,
looks a lot like
being a good neighbor.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Planted by the Water, “good neighbor” (Psalm 15:1–5) slows us down at the quiet centerpiece of “good neighbor” to remind us: “holiness, it turns out, looks a lot like being a good neighbor.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: pleasant places
paintings.epigraph: “The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places.”
paintings.poem:
the surveyor's lines
fell on good ground.

my little plot.
my portion.
my cup.

not the biggest field in Israel.
but it's mine,
and God is in it.

contentment
isn't having more.
it's seeing
that what you have
was measured out
by a kind hand.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “pleasant places” (Psalm 16:5–11), what would you talk about after reading, “it's seeing that what you have was measured out by a kind hand”?

paintings.title: the apple of your eye
paintings.epigraph: “Keep me as the apple of your eye. Hide me under the shadow of your wings”
paintings.poem:
the apple of your eye—
the old phrase for the pupil,
the part you protect
without thinking.

keep me like that.

and hide me
in the shadow of your wings,
the way a small bird
disappears under its mother
when the hawk goes over.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the cool shadow of the rock: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “the apple of your eye”—“and hide me in the shadow of your wings, the way a small bird disappears under its mother when the hawk goes over”?

paintings.title: my lamp
paintings.epigraph: “For you will light my lamp, Yahweh. My God will light up my darkness.”
paintings.poem:
rock. fortress. deliverer.
shield. horn. high tower.

David runs out of words
for what God has been to him.

and then the smallest one:
you light my lamp.

not the sun.
not a bonfire.
enough light
for the room I'm in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the small oil lamp in the dark in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “enough light for the room I'm in” (Psalm 18:1–28)?

paintings.title: the sky is preaching
paintings.epigraph: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”
paintings.poem:
the sky is preaching.
every day.
no words,
and yet
its voice goes out to the whole earth.

the sun comes up
like a bridegroom
from his tent.

look up.
the sermon
has already started.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Psalm 19:1–6, the story turns on the still, unhurried voice—and ends with, “the sermon has already started.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: chariots
paintings.epigraph: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we trust in the name of Y ahweh our God.”
paintings.poem:
chariots were the tanks
of the ancient world.

and horses.
and armies.
and money.

and we
trust a name.

the chariots rusted.
the horses are gone.
the name
still stands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Psalm 20:7–8 points us to the name by which He calls you and whispers, “the chariots rusted. the name still stands.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: the best gift
paintings.epigraph: “Y ou make him glad with joy in your presence.”
paintings.poem:
the king had a crown of gold,
victories,
long life.

and the best line
in his song:

you make him glad
with joy
in your presence.

all the rest were gifts.
this
was the giver.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “all the rest were gifts. this was the giver.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: forsaken
paintings.epigraph: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
paintings.poem:
Jesus prayed these words
on the cross.

the psalm he quoted
starts in the dark:
why have you forsaken me?

but it doesn't end there.
it ends:
he has not despised the afflicted.
he heard.

when he cried the first line,
he knew
the last one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “when he cried the first line, he knew the last one” (Psalm 22:1–24) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: through the valley
paintings.epigraph: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me.”
paintings.poem:
not around the valley.
through it.

he never promised
we'd skip the shadows.

he promised
to be there in them—
rod and staff,
close enough to hear.

and on the far side:
a table,
oil,
a full cup,

and goodness
following me home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “through the valley” (Psalm 23:1–6): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “and on the far side: a table, oil, a full cup, and goodness following me home”?

paintings.title: lift up your heads
paintings.epigraph: “Lift up your heads, you gates!”
paintings.poem:
the whole earth
is his,
and everyone in it.

and still
he knocks at the gates.

lift up your heads.
open wide.
the King of glory
is coming in.

every closed door in you—
he's asking
to be let in.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Psalm 24:1–10 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “every closed door in you— he's asking to be let in” in your own story?

paintings.title: teach me
paintings.epigraph: “Show me your ways, Y ahweh. T each me your paths.”
paintings.poem:
not a map.
a teacher.

show me.
teach me.
lead me.

I'll wait all day,
the psalm says.

the path isn't
something you find once.
it's something you're taught,
step by step,
by someone walking beside you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “teach me” (Psalm 25:4–5), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet centerpiece of “teach me” after reading, “it's something you're taught, step by step, by someone walking beside you”?

paintings.title: I love your house
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh, I love the habitation of your house, the place where your glory dwells.”
paintings.poem:
some people go to God's house
because they have to.

David went
because he loved it:
the place where your glory lives.

like a child
who runs ahead
to Grandma's door.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“some people go to God's house because they have to”) and the closing thought (“like a child who runs ahead to Grandma's door”), what is Psalm 26:8 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: one thing
paintings.epigraph: “One thing I have asked of Yahweh”
paintings.poem:
if you could ask God
for one thing—
just one—

David already chose:

to live in your house
all my days,
to look at your beauty,
to sit with you
and ask questions.

not the gift.
the Giver's company.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Planted by the Water, “one thing” (Psalm 27:4) slows us down at the quiet centerpiece of “one thing” to remind us: “not the gift. the Giver's company.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: a song
paintings.epigraph: “My heart has trusted in him, and I am helped.”
paintings.poem:
my strength.
my shield.

I trusted,
and I was helped.

and so—
the natural next thing—
a song.

gratitude
wants a melody.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “a song” (Psalm 28:6–7), what would you talk about after reading, “I trusted, and I was helped. gratitude wants a melody”?

paintings.title: the voice on the waters
paintings.epigraph: “Y ahweh’s voice is on the waters. The God of glory thunders”
paintings.poem:
thunder over the sea.
cedars cracking.
the desert shaking.

that's his voice,
the psalm says.

and after all that power,
the last line:

the Lord gives strength to his people.
the Lord blesses his people
with peace.

the voice that shakes the world
speaks peace
to you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the open wilderness road: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “the voice on the waters”—“the voice that shakes the world speaks peace to you”?

paintings.title: morning
paintings.epigraph: “W eeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.”
paintings.poem:
weeping may stay the night—
like a guest
who won't leave.

but it's only a guest.

joy
comes in the morning.

you turned my mourning
into dancing,
he says.

the night is real.
so is the morning.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the quiet centerpiece of “morning” in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “the night is real. so is the morning” (Psalm 30:5–11)?

paintings.title: my times
paintings.epigraph: “My times are in your hand.”
paintings.poem:
my times—
my days, my years,
the good seasons and the waiting ones,
my first day and my last—

are in your hand.

not in the enemy's.
not in chance.
not even in mine.

into your hands
I commit my spirit:
Jesus prayed this psalm too.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Psalm 31:5–15, the story turns on your own two hands—and ends with, “into your hands I commit my spirit: Jesus prayed this psalm too.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: said out loud
paintings.epigraph: “Blessed is he whose disobedience is forgiven, whose sin is covered.”
paintings.poem:
when I kept silent,
my bones wasted away.

the weight of it
all day
and all night.

then I said it—
out loud, to God.

and he forgave.

the heaviest thing you carry
might be the thing
you haven't said yet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Psalm 32:1–5 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “said out loud” and whispers, “the heaviest thing you carry might be the thing you haven't said yet.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: a new song
paintings.epigraph: “Sing to him a new song. Play skillfully with a shout of joy!”
paintings.poem:
a new song—

not because the old ones wore out,
but because
his mercies are new
every morning,

and new mercy
deserves
new music.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “a new song— not because the old ones wore out, but because his mercies are new every morning, and new mercy deserves new music.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: near
paintings.epigraph: “Yahweh is near to those who have a broken heart”
paintings.poem:
David wrote this
after pretending to be mad
to escape a king.

not his finest hour.

and still:
taste and see.
the Lord is good.

and this:
he is near
the brokenhearted.

not far from them.
near.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “and this: he is near the brokenhearted. not far from them. near” (Psalm 34:8–18) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: who is like you?
paintings.epigraph: “who delivers the poor from him who is too strong for him”
paintings.poem:
all my bones will say it:
who is like you?

you rescue the weak
from the one
who's too strong for them.

every bully in history
learns this
eventually:

the poor
have a defender.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “who is like you?” (Psalm 35:10): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “every bully in history learns this eventually: the poor have a defender”?

paintings.title: in your light
paintings.epigraph: “For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.”
paintings.poem:
with you is the fountain of life.
in your light
we see light.

we don't see him
by the light
of our own cleverness.

he is the light
we see
everything else by.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Psalm 36:7–9 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “he is the light we see everything else by” in your own story?

paintings.title: don't fret
paintings.epigraph: “Rest in Yahweh, and wait patiently for him. Don’t fret”
paintings.poem:
don't fret,
the psalm says,
again and again.

don't burn yourself up
watching the wicked get ahead.

rest.
wait.
delight yourself in the Lord.

the grass that grows fast
withers fast.
you're planted
for something longer.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “don't fret” (Psalm 37:1–7), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet centerpiece of “don't fret” after reading, “you're planted for something longer”?

paintings.title: not hidden
paintings.epigraph: “Lord, all my desire is before you. My groaning is not hidden from you.”
paintings.poem:
this is a sick man's prayer.
pain,
friends keeping their distance,
guilt he can't shake.

and one sentence
that holds him up:

my longing is before you.
my groaning
isn't hidden.

he knows.
before you find the words,
he knows.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“this is a sick man's prayer”) and the closing thought (“before you find the words, he knows”), what is Psalm 38:9–15 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: a handbreadth
paintings.epigraph: “show me my end, what is the measure of my days. Let me know how frail I am.”
paintings.poem:
you've made my days
a few handbreadths.

a breath.
a shadow.
a guest passing through.

it isn't morbid.
it's clarifying.

when life is short,
you stop hoarding
and start
hoping in him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Planted by the Water, “a handbreadth” (Psalm 39:4–12) slows us down at the cool shadow of the rock to remind us: “when life is short, you stop hoarding and start hoping in him.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: out of the pit
paintings.epigraph: “He brought me up also out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay. He set my feet on a rock”
paintings.poem:
I waited, and waited,
and he bent down
and heard.

he pulled me
out of the mud,
set my feet on rock,

and put a new song
in my mouth.

and many will see,
the psalm says,
and trust him too.

your rescue
is someone else's reason
to hope.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “out of the pit” (Psalm 40:1–3), what would you talk about after reading, “your rescue is someone else's reason to hope”?

paintings.title: amen and amen
paintings.epigraph: “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting and to everlasting! Amen and amen.”
paintings.poem:
the first book of Psalms
began with a blessing
on the one who stays near the water.

it ends
with a blessing
on the one who notices the poor.

and then,
like a congregation standing up
at the end:

blessed be the Lord,
forever and forever.
amen and amen.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet centerpiece of “amen and amen”: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “amen and amen”—“and then, like a congregation standing up at the end: blessed be the Lord, forever and forever. amen and amen”?
